value.text: Jennifer Eckhart, a popular podcaster and former associate producer at Fox Business, died by suicide at her home in Hobe Sound on Saturday morning, according to the Martin County sheriff. Sheriff John Budensiek said he usually doesn't comment on suicides but decided to speak publicly about Eckhart’s death to address conspiracy theories suggesting she had been murdered. "Looking at the scene and going through the investigation, we spent a lot of time. We investigated it as if it was a homicide. Unfortunately, she took her life at her own hands," Budensiek said. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Eckhart gained notoriety after accusing a Fox News anchor of raping her. Investigators said she had family and friends who tried to help her, but she had been in and out of mental health facilities and had stopped taking her medications. If you'd like to talk to someone at 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, you can dial 211. If you'd like to text the helpline, you can message your ZIP code to 898211. Elizabeth Burrows, director of development and communications with 211 Palm Beach and Treasure Coast, emphasized the tragedy of suicide and encouraged those struggling to seek help. "Every death by suicide is a tragedy," Burrows said. She noted that anyone in crisis can call 211 or 988, which are available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to provide resources or someone to talk to. "You'd be surprised at how often just having someone who's there to listen can help someone make it through their darkest moments," Burrows said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Burrows also stressed the importance of being present and asking questions when supporting someone who may be struggling. Asking about it does not make suicide more of a risk for them. If anything, it lets that person know that they are not alone," she said. "The one answer I can always give is to never give up. As long as someone is still here, there is still an opportunity to support and assist them." The sheriff said Eckhart’s death remains an open investigation as they await toxicology results, but he emphasized that all evidence points to suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available by dialing 211 or 988 for confidential support and resources. If you or someone you know needs help, you can talk with the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or sending a text message to 988, or you can chat online here.

38-year-old Darrel Abbey is facing multiple charges after Martin County deputies say he barricaded himself inside a Palm City guest house during an hours-long standoff with law enforcement Saturday . According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Abbey was taken into custody after SWAT officers and hostage negotiators spent hours trying to convince him to surrender. Deputies said they were initially called to a home along SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road for a domestic-related incident. Investigators say the situation escalated when Abbey, who deputies say was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property. "I was pretty scared because it doesn't usually happen in our neighborhood," said 11-year-old Gavin Ryan, who lives next door. See also: Routine warrant leads to shocking major animal cruelty bust in Lake Worth Ryan's mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded. Deputies said hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. "[Gavin's] mom told me about it, and I was like, 'Whoa,' Tracy said. "I've never heard about a shooting in someone's neighborhood." Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and is facing three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

More details are being released about a road rage incident in Port St. Lucie that escalated into a shooting Thursday evening, resulting in one man being injured and both drivers arrested on felony charges. Lucie police received a 911 call around 6:30 p.m. reporting gunshots in a residential neighborhood near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace. "Gunshots in front of my house," a caller said during the emergency call. The caller also described the aftermath of the shooting. "I heard it, and then I saw a guy raising his hands up and said he had blood on his hands," the caller said. Investigators said the altercation began as a misunderstanding during a lane change and merge near SW Crosstown Parkway. The situation escalated into a physical confrontation when 41-year-old Dean Plotts exited his vehicle, approached 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, who was seated in his car, and punched him through the window. "He stepped out of his vehicle, approached the other man who was seated inside his vehicle, and punched him inside his vehicle, so now he's breaking the plane of the window," the Port St. Lucie police chief Leo Niemczyk said. "Therefore, entering, which makes it a burglary of the conveyance with the intention of committing a crime, being battery by punching the other individual who is seated inside the vehicle." Plotts then returned to his vehicle, but the confrontation escalated further. "Almost makes it back to his vehicle and starts getting fire on," Niemczyk said. Police said Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Both men were arrested, with Plotts facing charges for initiating the physical altercation and Kukielka for firing his weapon. When asked if Kukielka’s actions could be considered self-defense, Niemczyk said, "It's not self-defense at that point. If Plotts had been coming at him at that point, the shooting may well have been justified, but it was actually just the reverse. He was fleeing from him." Both men are now facing felony charges. Because one thought the other one may have cut the other one off when they were both turning into the same roadway. Again, no reason to be facing felony charges; let it go, let it go," Niemczyk said. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. Guaca Go has officially expanded west with the opening of its new Royal Palm Beach restaurant on National Guacamole Day.The South Florida-based fast-casual restaurant opened Wednesday at 10101 Southern Blvd., Unit 190, marking the fourth Palm Beach County location for the growing Florida Fresh-Mex brand. According to Guaca Go, franchisees Fab Nunez and Jessie Sequeira locally own and operate the new restaurant, which also opened the company's Tequesta location earlier this year.The restaurant will hold a ribbon-cutting ceremony at noon Wednesday, offering $5 bowls from noon to 3 p.m. as part of the grand opening celebration.Guaca Go said the Royal Palm Beach expansion brings the brand farther west into communities including Royal Palm Beach and Wellington as the company continues growing across Palm Beach County.The restaurant specializes in customizable bowls, burritos and salads centered around guacamole made fresh to order in front of customers. Guaca Go said its menu includes gluten-free, vegan-friendly, and seed-oil-free options."Our shift lead ties an apron on him and walks him down the line building a Build-Your-Own bowl start to finish," the company said in describing one of the demonstrations featured during WPTV's "Shining A Light" broadcast.The company was founded in 2017 by Carson and Amber Bennett as a roadside guacamole stand in the Florida Keys before expanding into brick-and-mortar restaurants in Palm Beach County.In addition to Wednesday’s grand opening promotions, Guaca Go planned two additional community-focused events:Thursday, Sept. 17: Giveback Day benefiting Roots and Wings, with $1 from every bowl, burrito or salad donated to the literacy nonprofit.Friday, Sept. 18: Community Appreciation Day featuring 50% discounts for first responders, nurses, teachers and students.According to Guaca Go, Roots and Wings provides free literacy instruction to more than 1,600 students across 24 Title I elementary schools in Palm Beach County.As more restaurant concepts continue expanding into western Palm Beach County, openings like this reflect the area’s ongoing residential and commercial growth. Local businesses are increasingly targeting communities west of Interstate 95 as population growth continues across the region.Guaca Go Royal Palm Beach is open daily from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

Following reporting on the closures of JetRide and Carefree Boat Club locations in Palm Beach County and on the Treasure Coast, two former employees are now speaking out about their experiences working at the clubs.Zachariah Rowland is a former training captain for Carefree Boat Club in Fort Pierce, who also worked as a dockhand at other locations in Florida, but was later terminated.WATCH BELOW: Ex-employees speak out after boat club closuresRowland reached out to WPTV after our reporting on the closures and the issues members experienced at the docks.Rowland said employees were left to face frustrated members without support from management."We're right there with the members, getting essentially yelled at by the members. They're upset, they're frustrated, rightfully so, and we would have to take the brunt of it, not JetRide or Carefree management." Rowland said.Despite the difficult conditions, Rowland said the members were what he loved about the job."The members were the reason why I kept going," Rowland said. "It was a hard place to work." Thomas Margait worked at JetRide in Stuart and at other locations in South Florida. He said employees tried to do right by members, but leadership let them down."We did try to provide a good service, and, unfortunately, I feel management failed us," Margait said.Margait said members deserve accountability."They need to have an answer or a resolution," Margait said.On Sept. 9, JetRide and Carefree Boat Club sent emails to members saying that effective Sept. 1, they ceased operations, citing rising costs and weather disruptions.WPTV has continued to reach out to the owners of JetRide and Carefree Boat Club about these concerns since earlier this month, and we're still working on a response.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Democrat David Jolly says he will not debate Republican Byron Donalds before the Nov. 3 election, leaving Florida's two major-party nominees for governor arguing over why they have yet to share a stage.Jolly announced his decision Sunday, accusing Donalds of acting in bad faith and arguing that a debate would deepen political division. Donalds says Jolly is avoiding scrutiny of his property insurance proposal and other policies.WATCH BELOW: Jolly rules out debates with Donalds, setting off new clash"I think he's acting with bad faith and continues to peddle lies. And Rev, you can't debate a liar," Jolly told Rev. Al Sharpton on MS NOW over the weekend.The campaigns had accepted different debate invitations, but never agreed to the same events. Jolly accepted proposed forums with CBS Miami's Jim DeFede and the Tampa Tiger Bay Club. Donalds announced he had accepted three other events involving Spectrum News and Florida A&M University, News4Jax, and Telemundo and NBC 6.Donalds' campaign said its proposed debates would feature two podiums and no audience. Jolly's campaign said it learned of those arrangements through a news release."Byron refused them and instead set his own rules by press release," Jolly said in a statement about the invitations he had accepted.Donalds responded by pointing to Jolly's earlier willingness to debate him."I said 3 debates. Yesterday, Jolly said no debates. Who's the liar Dave?" Donalds wrote in a post on X.Jolly's statement also linked to fact-checks of Donalds' campaign attacks. In one, PolitiFact rated false a claim that Jolly wants higher taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.The dispute comes after Donalds declined calls to debate his Republican primary opponents. At a Florida Chamber event, he compared the campaign to applying for a job."If I'm applying for a job, it's not my responsibility to help my competitor get a job interview," Donalds said.Jolly is now citing that reasoning, saying it is not his job to give Donalds a platform. He said his campaign has held more than 300 town halls and community meetings and will continue meeting voters and conducting online outreach.Political analyst Dr. Susan MacManus said debates offer candidates free exposure and give voters, including those still undecided, a chance to compare the contenders directly."You'll have an unfiltered look at yourself and your opponent side by side," she said.MacManus said declining interest in politics and lengthy televised events can reduce debates' appeal. Candidates may see more value in knocking on doors, holding town halls or doing local interviews.Artificial intelligence and social media add another consideration, she said. Misleading posts and manipulated material can spread while a debate is underway, potentially shaping perceptions before the candidates leave the stage.But refusing to participate can also alienate voters, MacManus said."It still looks bad to say that you don't want to debate an opponent," she said.If the candidates do not meet, it would be Florida's first governor's election without a televised debate in more than 50 years, according to the Tampa Bay Times.

Delray Beach Mayor Tom Carney says he's not in favor of raising the city millage rate on the city's homeowners, since taxes may already be going up because of rising property values."Even if we do nothing, we just keep the current millage, the residents are going to pay almost 7% more in taxes," he says.WATCH: Delray Beach mayor says he's against raising property tax rateCity commissioners will decide on the tax rate on Tuesday.According to Carney, Delray Beach benefits from rising property values, a busy business district on Atlantic Avenue and new developments in the pipeline."We know they're gonna be on the tax rolls in 2027, we know they're gonna be on the tax rolls in 2028."Under state law, Carney is not taking a position on Amendment 3, the voter referendum that aims to raise the Homestead Exemption and lower property tax bills across Florida.He admits if it passes there will be an impact, and the city has placed signs reminding residents of what property taxes mean for the city."I think that there was an overall sense that we need to rein in these expenses and we need to force municipalities to do what others are doing, which is figure out ways to save money," Carney says.

Crews in the Indian Trail Improvement District are working early mornings and late nights to pump down elevated water levels after days of heavy rain, but officials say garbage clogging drainage canals is making a tough job even harder.Board President Elizabeth Accomando said Monday that while "pumping and dumping," as her crews call it, has been continuous since last week's flooding, water levels in key impoundments remain above where they should be.WATCH BELOW: Trash clogs canals, prompting more flooding concerns"The south impoundment, we're almost a foot above where we like to be, and the north impoundment is still about almost 2 feet above where we'd like it to be," Accomando said. "They're going to continually pump."Lightning and fresh rainfall have slowed progress, but Accomando said an avoidable problem is also hindering the system: trash and yard debris blocking pipes and canals.Standing along one of the district's canals, Accomando pointed to items floating in the water as an example of what crews are pulling out."As you can see, we've got the cooler. It looks like we've got some other personal items, a lot of bottles, just a lot of trash that maybe people are just throwing out their car window as they're going by, or it ends up in the swale and then flows through, and this is where it ends up," she said.On one property, crews found an entire bag of softballs shoved into a pipe. Other times, they've hauled out deflated balls, toys and even coconuts."That clogs up the whole system," Accomando said. "The water backflows into people's properties, so we're up against that as well. Cleaning it out."When crews have to stop to clear blockages, it delays efforts to keep water moving out of flooded neighborhoods.Accomando stressed that while the district manages more than 1,000 miles of canals, swales and ditches, residents have an important role in keeping water flowing."People don't think it's their responsibility," she said. "It's still your land, it's still your residence. So again, if you're able, just be mindful of those things."She urged residents to rake up vegetation left behind after curbside pickup and to keep swales clear so debris doesn't wash into drainage pipes."If you've got a lot of vegetation on the swale for SWA to pick it up, they leave a lot of that debris behind. Try and rake it up if you're able to, because eventually that's going to end up in the pipe and it's going to clog the pipe," she said.The district office, which serves about 17,000 resident-owned lots, is fielding "hundreds and hundreds of calls," she added, and staff are working to return voicemails and emails as quickly as possible."You have to have a little patience right now because we're trying to accommodate so many people at once," she said.Accomando said newer residents, especially those who moved in over the last few relatively dry years, may not realize that the community was intentionally designed to hold water on individual properties."The way that The Acreage was designed, it's designed for you to hold water on your property," she said. "The houses are higher than the lot. You've got low areas that are depressed. The water is going to remain there until the ground can absorb it, which you want because we have to recharge our aquifers. We're all on well water."Swales may move water in some areas and simply hold it in others, she said, but all of it is part of a larger system that has to function together."Water is like gold these days," Accomando said. "You don't want to get rid of any more than you have to."The original design for the area dates back to the 1950s, long before anyone envisioned how large the community — or its surrounding development — would become.Historically, house pads were raised slightly and ponds were dug on lots as a critical drainage feature."You want to have a pond. You shouldn't fill your pond in," Accomando said. "It's all part of the system."As building requirements changed, Palm Beach County began requiring higher house pads and engineered drainage plans to keep water on-site. Problems arise, she said, when residents bring in fill or build structures without following those plans or constructing berms to contain runoff."What we see happening, the higher properties are sending the water to the neighbors who are lower, and they're not building their berm, or they're removing their berm," she said.Accomando described a recent complaint from a resident whose neighbor built a shed that met distance requirements from the property line but sat on an elevated pad with no berm."All that water and all that sand from his base is all washing in and creating a major issue for the next-door neighbor," she said. "We all live here together. We have to work together and be mindful that what we're doing is affecting the person down the line."With large portions of some yards still underwater, mosquitoes are an inevitable concern."When you've got a good portion of your yard [underwater], what are you going to do?" Accomando said.She recommended residents dump standing water in small containers, like garbage can lids and plant saucers, and use commercially available mosquito "dunks" or larvicide products in larger areas of standing water."The wading birds will come in. They'll eat a lot of it," she said, but noted the district cannot eliminate mosquitoes and mosquito-borne disease risks entirely. A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon.Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. Losing someone you love can change everything.For Stacey Comer, that loss came in 2018 when her husband, Chris, died following complications from a kidney transplant.WATCH ‘You Are Not Alone’: PSL woman turns grief into community for othersAs she learned to navigate life without him, Comer also began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection.She started asking herself a simple question: “Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under?”That question became the foundation for Chris’s Place, a free, in-person grief support community Comer is now creating on the Treasure Coast.Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. She added that while friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated.“You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful,” Comer said.Chris’s Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through.The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next.Right now, Comer is creating Chris’s Place from the ground up.Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast — somewhere that feels comfortable and welcoming, where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief.“You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not,” Comer said.For Comer, Chris’s Place is rooted in the loss of her husband — but she hopes it can become something much bigger.She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief.The ultimate goal is to create a community where people don't have to navigate that journey by themselves. While grief may look different for everyone, Comer wants people to know one thing: They don't have to face it alone.For more information on the next free community grief meet-up, visit their website.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Boca Raton native Frankie Harris is making a name for himself in professional golf, winning a Korn Ferry Tour title just months into his pro career and setting his sights on the PGA Tour.Harris grew up with golf in his blood. Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Florida's Treasure Coast earned its name from Spanish coins that washed ashore centuries ago — and the legendary treasure hunters who came to collect them.Melvin Fisher-Abt is the grandson and namesake of one of America's most celebrated treasure hunters, Mel Fisher."I was born in 1997 and Mel passed in 1998 and out of all of the grandkids I was given the namesake Mel and I feel really connected to my grandfather in that way — definitely have big shoes to fill," Fisher-Abt said.His grandfather was a man whose dedication and determination rewrote the history books. His discoveries were so remarkable that Johnny Carson invited him to share his story with millions of viewers on "The Tonight Show.'Mel Fisher walked on stage wearing one of his favorite finds — a gold wedding chain."That's how he would look when he was sitting at the bar — draped in gold chains with gold bars," Fisher-Abt said.But before the fame and fortune came persistence, perseverance, and personal loss.Mel Fisher made his first discovery off the coast of Vero Beach, where over 1,000 gold coins were unearthed from the sunken 1715 Spanish Treasure Fleet."Gold is a noble metal and will be just as shiny as the day it went down — gold shines forever is what my grandfather used to say," Fisher-Abt said.In the 1600s and 1700s, Spanish fleets sailed annually from Spain to the Caribbean with a threefold mission."They were trying to extract wealth from the new world and bring it back to Spain to fund European wars and debts — they were trying to promote Catholicism," Fisher-Abt said. "They were trying to conquer land for the kingdom of Spain — so 'God, Glory and Gold' was their mission."When some of those fleets shipwrecked in major storms, Florida became a hotspot for treasure hunters. One of them — the Spanish galleon Nuestra Señora de Atocha — sank in a powerful hurricane in 1622 off the coast of Key West.Mel Fisher moved his family and crew to the Florida Keys specifically to search for the Atocha's buried treasure."Initially, he believed they would find it in six months and after six months he said alright maybe a year — and after a year he said alright maybe we'll be here for awhile," Fisher-Abt said. "He was an eternal optimist."In 1973, Mel Fisher found a 14-foot galleon anchor he believed was from the Atocha."Everyday he would wake up and say today is the day — cause he believed it in his bones that one musket ball and one silver coin and an anchor would lead to a huge pile of treasure," Fisher-Abt said.It was another 12 years before Mel and his team found the massive Atocha "Mother Lode" — an estimated $400 million to $450 million in gold, silver, coins, and emeralds.But before the big find came the greatest test of Mel's determination, when tragedy struck. In 1975, their salvage vessel capsized and three crew members perished, including his eldest son."If there was ever a stopping point that my grandfather really considered giving up the hunt losing my uncle Dirk was that point in time," Fisher-Abt said.Yet Mel chose to honor his son's memory by continuing the quest they shared."When he did get back to the site it was a renewed sense of finishing the job," Fisher-Abt said.He found the Atocha's main treasure pile exactly 10 years to the day after his greatest loss. The search continues to this day."Along the way we've recovered all kinds of artifacts — religious artifacts — some of them are very intricate some are preserved very well deep in the mud," Fisher-Abt said.According to Fisher-Abt, there is still much more to be found."The research that's been done and the work that's been done by the people before us is true and faithful and that everything they've done will pan out for us — there is another 20 tons of silver at the end of the rainbow," Fisher-Abt said.For more information about Mel Fisher's Treasures, click here.Watch "Finding Florida" each Sunday at 10 a.m.

A confrontation in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot ended with a man shot in the upper torso and later facing charges. 19, officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Blvd., where they found Christopher Harris suffering from gunshot wounds to his upper torso, according to a news release. The shooting led to a heavy law enforcement investigation outside the business , with crime scene tape around the restaurant. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm. PSLPD said interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order, police said. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris allegedly followed him outside. Police said surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso, according to PSLPD. Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket, police said. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor, according to PSLPD. He was charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction. Police said Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail once he is medically released from the hospital.

Lucie County staff are providing updates to commissioners tonight on the removal of automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-maintained roads after a vote earlier this month. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said letters were sent earlier this week to all permit holders, notifying them of the decision and giving them 30 days to remove the cameras. "Earlier this week, letters went out to all the permit holders, whether some of those were permits were submitted on the behalf of law enforcement agencies, some were directly manufacturers of those cameras. So, they were notified this week and have 30 days to remove those cameras from the St. Lucie County right-of-ways," Gill said. County right-of-ways include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. Gill said there were about 50 to 55 permits issued for the cameras. "I'm sure the permit owners going to want to do that because...I'm sure there's value to these cameras that they don't want damaged, and they did the installations, so we're going to make sure they comply with the 30-day rule, or we'll begin the process of removing them ourselves," Gill said. French football star Kylian Mbappé has signed a new sponsorship deal with sportswear brand On, following the end of his roughly 20-year relationship with Nike.The Swiss-based company announced Friday that Mbappé will become a global ambassador for On and “work directly with On’s product teams” on footwear and apparel. This marks a significant entry for the company into the growing football apparel space that has long been dominated by Adidas and Nike.Mbappé, who at just 27 years old is the World Cup’s all-time goal scorer, will bring his “elite perspective” into the development and testing of future football products, including On’s Lightspray technology that makes shoes with the help of robots.RELATED STORY | These Nike shoes have a motor — and could change how you run foreverThe length of the deal wasn’t disclosed, but an On spokesperson told CNN that the financial agreement includes both cash and equity components.On was founded in 2010, but grew in recognition when Swiss tennis star Roger Federer became an investor in 2019. The brand, initially known for its running and marathon shoes, then expanded into training and tennis shoes. The company represents Ben Shelton, who was a finalist at this year’s US Open.Signing Mbappé, who currently plays forward for Real Madrid, signals that On is looking to further encroach into its larger competitors’ territory.RELATED STORY | Caitlin Clark lands $28M endorsement deal with NikeDuring the recent World Cup, Adidas outfitted Spain and Argentina, both finalists, as well as manufactured the tournament’s balls. The German company recently reported record revenue, driven by sales of football jerseys during the month-long tournament.Nike, however, has been less than fortunate: Its shares are hovering around a 12-year low as it deals with a series of problems that CEO Elliott Hill hasn’t been able to fix, including customers shopping at trendier brands like On.On is planning to shake up the football category, writing in a press release that it’s “bringing a new energy to the culture that surrounds it.”To do that, On also signed Thierry Henry, another French legend, as its new director of Football. It also expanded its relationship with Sydney Schertenleib, a Swiss soccer player that plays for FC Barcelona’s women’s team.

Christian McCaffrey put himself in some elite company with two short touchdown runs.McCaffrey's two 1-yard TDs in a 35-13 win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday made him the fourth-fastest player in the Super Bowl era to reach 100 career touchdowns and the third player ever with at least 50 TDs with two franchises.“It means a lot,” McCaffrey said. “It's a blessing to be able to play this game and stuff like that is always cool. But it's always about the team and showing up and doing your job.”IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell agrees on a 4-year contract extensionMcCaffrey didn't have to do a lot on Sunday, a day when Brock Purdy and the rest of the offense was clicking at such a high level that the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five drives.McCaffrey started it with a 1-yard run in the first quarter and capped the scoring for San Francisco late in the third when he scored again from 1-yard out. He finished with 23 yards on 10 carries and four catches for 43 yards.“CMC, he’s just the GOAT,” linebacker Fred Warner said. “GOATs do things like that. It’s just another day at the office for old Christian. But nobody works harder on their craft and is as dedicated to the game as Christian. Everything that he does, he’s earned it and he’s only going to continue to keep getting better.”The scores gave him 64 rushing touchdowns and 36 receiving in 114 regular-season games for Carolina and San Francisco. Only LaDainian Tomlinson (89 games), Emmitt Smith (93) and Shaun Alexander (96) got to 100 TDs faster in the Super Bowl era.McCaffrey, who has 50 touchdowns with both Carolina and San Francisco, joined Marshall Faulk and Randy Moss as the only players to score at least 50 TDs with two franchises.“It’s kind of crazy to hear that,” McCaffrey said. “I watched all those guys growing up. Marshall Faulk was somebody that I’ve probably seen every single snap he’s played. I don’t take it for granted. Randy Moss I played with a ton of times with Madden growing up. Those are huge, huge honors.”MORE NFL NEWS | NFL ends the Pro Bowl game, but players will still be honored as Pro BowlersMcCaffrey's career is full of noteworthy accomplishments already. He became the third player ever with at least 1,000 yards rushing and receiving in the same season in 2019 with Carolina, has earned first-team All-Pro honors in three seasons, and won the AP NFL Offensive Player of the Year in 2023 and Comeback Player of the Year in 2025.“It’s crazy. I grew up watching him in high school and stuff when he was at Stanford and then the Panthers and then to be a teammate with him and be there when he scored his 100th touchdown was insane,” Purdy said. "It’s really cool to think about that. To be on his team and be a teammate with him and go and help him do what he wants to do with his career and just be there and feed him the ball and stuff, it’s an honor for me."

A Fort Pierce man was arrested after a raid Friday by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, worth several million dollars. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce. The subject of the investigation, Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody. Saunders, a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation, also had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. Afterward, Saunders faced additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0j4igLYhtX4QpfPCZhHkYeREcfiqd9eehsAoAcjVwDWTipnXHZNWyrJLe6gbwukcvl The search resulted in the seizure of approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams, the sheriff's office said. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, depending heavily on its purity, geographic location, and whether it is sold as wholesale powder or broken down into counterfeit pills, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine in the U.S. ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. “4.5 kilos of fentanyl are 4.5 kilos that will not reach our streets," Sheriff Richard Del Tro said. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit. I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Losing someone you love can change everything.For Stacey Comer, that loss came in 2018 when her husband, Chris, died following complications from a kidney transplant.WATCH ‘You Are Not Alone’: PSL woman turns grief into community for othersAs she learned to navigate life without him, Comer also began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection.She started asking herself a simple question: “Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under?”That question became the foundation for Chris’s Place, a free, in-person grief support community Comer is now creating on the Treasure Coast.Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. She added that while friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated.“You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful,” Comer said.Chris’s Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through.The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next.Right now, Comer is creating Chris’s Place from the ground up.Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast — somewhere that feels comfortable and welcoming, where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief.“You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not,” Comer said.For Comer, Chris’s Place is rooted in the loss of her husband — but she hopes it can become something much bigger.She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief.The ultimate goal is to create a community where people don't have to navigate that journey by themselves. While grief may look different for everyone, Comer wants people to know one thing: They don't have to face it alone.For more information on the next free community grief meet-up, visit their website.

Before an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City , a man allegedly threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend after she went to his home to check on him following their breakup, a new report reveals. According to an arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the ex-girlfriend of the suspect, Darrel Abbey, arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts, according to the report. The woman told investigators Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated. The arrest report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman, "I should die, you should kill me," while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey continued yelling at the woman while recording the interaction on his phone. The woman told investigators that Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed, according to the report. Investigators said Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey allegedly continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. The report says that when Abbey picked up the gun again, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now." Investigators said Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. As Abbey walked outside, the woman told investigators she heard several loud "pop" sounds. Abbey then returned inside to retrieve a rifle and allegedly tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey allegedly told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it. At some point during the incident, Abbey allegedly began cleaning the firearms and said, "I gotta wipe all my fingerprints off, I gotta get the gunshot residue off of my hands, I'm not going back to prison." The report says Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink, prompting the woman to begin recording him. Investigators who reviewed the video said Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he allegedly reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her. Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Investigators also said Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

Coast Guard has suspended its search for missing paddleboarder Matt Pawlowski, 48, who was last seen off Jupiter Inlet, pending new information."The decision to suspend an active search is one of the most difficult decisions we make, and it comes only after every reasonable effort to locate the missing person has been exhausted," Captain Frank Florio, commander of Coast Guard Sector Miami, said."Our crews and partner agencies searched tirelessly for Matt. The paddleboard was returned to local law enforcement.Over the course of the multi-day search, Coast Guard air and surface crews conducted extensive nighttime and daytime operations. Assets involved included Coast Guard Cutters Margaret Norvell, Robert Yered, Pablo Valent and Skipjack, along with HC-130 aircraft from Air Station Elizabeth City and Air Station Miami, and Station Lake Worth Inlet and Station Fort Pierce. Space Force also assisted in identifying search areas.Search efforts were based on Pawlowski's last-known position, drift patterns and possible routes.Anyone with information that may assist search efforts is asked to contact Coast Guard Sector Miami at 305-535-4472.

Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements.The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1.A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly — an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030, according to city documents. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach.To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. A former Fort Pierce police officer was arrested Tuesday after investigators say he repeatedly accessed law enforcement databases without a legitimate police purpose, including hundreds of searches involving a vehicle registered to his ex-girlfriend.Former Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested on four felony counts related to unauthorized computer access and was being held Tuesday at the St. Lucie County Jail on an $80,000 secured bond, Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith announced during an afternoon news conference.WATCH BELOW: Former Fort Pierce officer accused of Flock camera misuseSmith said the investigation began after members of the media contacted the department on Aug. 7 with information raising concerns about Crutchfield's possible misuse of the department's Flock automated license plate reader system.Crutchfield was placed on administrative leave that same day and immediately lost access to law enforcement systems. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk was a Queens, New York, police officer when terrorists attacked the World Trade Center on Sept. Ron DeSantis on Wednesday celebrated the completion of the C-23 Canal Estuary Discharge Diversion Project in Martin County, calling it part of the largest environmental restoration effort in U.S. history.The project, located at 10297 Southwest Martin Highway, will reroute excess water from the C-23 Canal away from the South Fork of the Saint Lucie River — where it had previously contributed to harmful algal blooms — and instead send it through a nearly 7-mile interconnect canal to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area.DeSantis was joined at the ribbon-cutting by Florida Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Alexis Lambert and South Florida Water Management District Executive Director Drew Bartlett, along with district board members Chairman Goss, Ronnie Bergeron, Ben Butler, Charlotte Roman, Tom Hurley and Robert Spotswood Jr.Since entering its operational testing phase in May, the project has diverted nearly 5 billion gallons of water away from the Saint Lucie Estuary. When operating at full capacity, the pump stations can fill an Olympic-size swimming pool in just under 6 minutes.Lambert said the project is projected to prevent 55,000 pounds of nitrogen and 14,000 pounds of phosphorus from entering the Saint Lucie River on average each year, and will divert 6.3 billion gallons of water from the river to the C-44 Reservoir and Stormwater Treatment Area."Florida's waterways are a deeply interconnected system and preventing these harmful discharges will further improve the health of the estuary and the lagoon," Lambert said.DeSantis said his administration has invested close to $10 billion in Everglades restoration and water quality since taking office in January 2019 — a figure he said has never been matched in state history. He cited reductions of 5.6 million pounds of nitrogen per year and nearly 1 million pounds of phosphorus per year as among the tangible results of those investments.DeSantis also highlighted progress on the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir south of Lake Okeechobee, which he said was originally scheduled for completion in 2034. Through a partnership with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers announced after President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, the project is now projected to be completed by 2029 and at nearly half the original federal cost estimate."Isn't that something — what you want — under budget, ahead of schedule," DeSantis said.The EAA reservoir is designed to store 78 billion gallons of water and deliver 270 billion to 470 billion gallons of clean freshwater each year to the Everglades and Florida Bay.Bartlett said the pump station at the C-23 project site is capable of moving 166 million gallons of water every day — comparable in capacity to Miami's drinking water system — and has been operational since May 14."We haven't had a lost summer since you've been in office, Governor," Bartlett said. Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The trial for Palm City dog trainer and boarder Nikki Camerlengo has been delayed until 2027 — at least the ninth continuance in a case that began more than two years ago.In court Wednesday morning, prosecutor Kristin Chase said one of the state's key witnesses is on medical disability and told Judge Elizabeth Metzger that doctors say she cannot testify until at least the end of January.That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be allowed to take the stand at trial. "This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count."At one point, an exchange between Metzger and Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, grew heated."Your Honor, it's of no fault of the defendant," Kaplan said."I'm not saying that," Metzger said."You're looking at me!" Kaplan said."I'm not saying that!" Metzger replied.Kaplan has asked the court to block testimony from both the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed the two necropsies and from lead investigator Detective Christine Polizzi."I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan told WPTV.The hearing to decide whether those witnesses can testify has not yet taken place.For Adele Kirk Csontos, the wait for justice started even before Camerlengo's arrest. She filed a police report after her dog, Mako, died following 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022."I was devastated. It's probably going to sound crazy, but I literally for two weeks I couldn't talk to my friends," Kirk Csontos said. "I felt responsible."Camerlengo was never charged in Mako's death — his necropsy was inconclusive. Necropsies of two other dogs concluded they died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest and charges."I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos said.Despite the ongoing delays, Kirk Csontos said she has not given up hope."I'm still hopeful. Believe it or not, I'm still hopeful that she will be held accountable," Kirk Csontos said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
