The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233. READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. He was booked into the St. Koch says oftentimes the pain is felt not just by the victims and dealers, but by the people around them. Many parents or family members feel guilty, like they didn't do enough or they couldn't. They say, "What could have been done differently?" So, they actually carry the guilt, Koch said. While state data points to a steady decline in overdose deaths since 2021, Koch says that addiction is still a rampant cycle. We're moving away from being in touch with who we are. We don't want to have any pain. We don't want to be bored. We want to be entertained. So these drugs come in, and who can compete with cocaine? CBS12 News has reached out to Port St. Lucie Police for comment and is working to confirm additional details.

A 42-year-old travel MRI technician was arrested after Port St. Lucie police said a patient reported she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI at HCA Florida St. Gabriel Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16 on a charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim, a first-degree felony, police said. Wasana Chesler is a former patient of St. Lucie Hospital and couldn't believe the news. That's very horrible," Chesler said. "That's very sad." The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital, 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. Police said the woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy. Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital’s assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. Monica Defoster said she's been to St. Lucie Hospital many times including on Thursday while visiting her husband. She calls the allegations disturbing. They should have more than one person in the MRI room," Defoster said. "You go to the hospital and don't expect something like that." The investigation remains active. Lucie Hospital has cooperated with investigators, police said. Lucie Hospital provided CBS12 News with the following statement: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient. A hospital spokesman told CBS12 no other complaints have been reported since Cruz stared working there late last month. Cruz's employer could not be reached for comment. He remains behind bars in Brevard County.

Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. Neighbors reported hearing gunfire at approximately 6:30 p.m. "OK, last night we were trying to put the kids down, and we just heard like two big pop pops," resident Ripley Crawford said. "All we saw was the cars were kind of already pulled to the side, and you could see there was like a crash of sorts." The Port St. Lucie Police Department determined the incident stemmed from a misunderstanding between two drivers following a lane change and merging near Southwest Crosstown Parkway. One driver believed he was being followed after the vehicles crossed paths, but investigators found no intentional following. One of the drivers, 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputy traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Later that night, traffic was rerouted as investigators gathered evidence at the scene. "The traffic was just nonstop because they closed California. My neighbor got a call from her daughter in Tennessee that said there was a shooting down here," resident Ernie Lampreda said. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, and dash cam footage that captured portions of the incident. Based on the evidence, witness information, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody, and the investigation remains ongoing. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

A Fort Pierce man was arrested after a raid Friday by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, worth several million dollars. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce. The subject of the investigation, Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody. Saunders, a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation, also had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. Afterward, Saunders faced additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0j4igLYhtX4QpfPCZhHkYeREcfiqd9eehsAoAcjVwDWTipnXHZNWyrJLe6gbwukcvl The search resulted in the seizure of approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams, the sheriff's office said. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, depending heavily on its purity, geographic location, and whether it is sold as wholesale powder or broken down into counterfeit pills, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine in the U.S. ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. “4.5 kilos of fentanyl are 4.5 kilos that will not reach our streets," Sheriff Richard Del Tro said. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit. I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff’s Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store. Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves’s shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski’s face. As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, “I wouldn’t do that if I were you.” The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times. Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves’s petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves’s federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied. Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that “the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant,” and confirmed that “there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause.” The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

This is causing the traffic to back up blocking the exit to the residents of Spinnaker Bay Dr. I have seen the police presence but parents are ignoring it" said the message.That tip led WPTV to Manatee Elementary School and the nearby Lake Charleston community.A mother named Michelle, who was picking up two of her children from school, said she understands why residents are frustrated."This is a pain in the butt if I lived in Lake Charleston," Michelle said. "It's a nightmare, it's a chaos of kids with a bunch of people loading right here and then some walking down here you never know what are crossing."Michelle said there are not enough places to park, but she chooses to park at a nearby approved county park and walk to the school because it takes about half as long as waiting in the traditional pick-up and drop-off line.She said the drop off look took her as long as two and a half hours, parking and walking took 15 minutes. To see whether the concerns matched what residents were reporting, WPTV photographer Johann Hoffend visited the area during morning drop-off hours.He observed cars and trucks pulled over along the roadway, including vehicles parked directly in front of signs stating "No Parking" and signs warning that drop-offs in travel lanes are prohibited.When WPTV returned during afternoon dismissal, a similar scene unfolded despite multiple no parking signs throughout Charleston Shores Blvd."I park in the grass right there, see the white car that's mine," said Scott Ross while picking up one of his students.Ross said he while he is using the park-and-walk method, he isn't a fan of it and has considered using the school's pick-up line instead, but agrees with Michelle that the line is too long."Almost better to put your kid on a bus, bus takes them right to our house," Ross said.The School District of Palm Beach County said safety must come before convenience."The District urges families and students to prioritize safety over convenience during drop-off and pick-up," the district said in a statement. Families with students who walk or bike are encouraged to use the county park parking lot next door to campus and access the school's east-side biker and walker entrance.The district also warned families not to use the nearby Public Storage facility as a parking or drop-off location."Please refrain from using the Public Storage facility (behind the Winn Dixie plaza) as a parking space or drop off location in the morning," the message states. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.WATCH BELOW: Man who killed Indian River Co. deputy to be executed in OctoberReaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Health officials have issued a blue-green algae health alert for an area of Lake Okeechobee after water samples detected harmful toxins. The Florida Department of Health in Martin County said the alert covers the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area and was issued in response to samples collected Sept. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County. Residents and visitors should use caution in and around the lake, officials said. People should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials also advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water, according to the department. Officials said contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure, health officials said. RELATED: 'Influence campaign': Okeechobee County leaders want to change Lake O's narrative Officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903 . Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222 . Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090 .

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. He was booked into the St. Koch says oftentimes the pain is felt not just by the victims and dealers, but by the people around them. While state data points to a steady decline in overdose deaths since 2021, Koch says that addiction is still a rampant cycle. We're moving away from being in touch with who we are. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. A Vero Beach animal hospital manager was arrested after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County, then abandoned them outdoors without care. Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, was arrested Sept. 15 on an active warrant charging her with two counts of animal abandonment, both first-degree misdemeanors, according to Indian River County court records. Animal Control investigators said Wesley, who works at Dr. Dan’s Animal Hospital , picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. Wesley reportedly told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver, but she would not identify that person, the affidavit said. The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident’s front door. Investigators said the cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. An investigator said Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number. According to the affidavit, she declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home. The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley’s description, wearing a Dr. Dan’s T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. The warrant alleges Wesley abandoned the cats on a public street without providing care, food, protection or shelter. A judge set bond at $250 per count, for a total of $500.

Martin County High School received another threat through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third bomb threat involving our campus this week, the school district said Friday afternoon. "I recognize that you have heard from me repeatedly this week regarding safety-related disruptions on our campus," Principal Lori Vogel said in a message to families. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. Vogel noted the seriousness of the threats. "Every threat must be taken seriously," the principal said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat." The message added: "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community. FortifyFL is an important safety resource. Students and families who become aware of a credible threat—or who have a legitimate reason to believe questionable, dangerous or criminal activity may be occurring—should continue to report that information through FortifyFL. Information about submitting a report is available on our school's and the School District's websites. "However, FortifyFL must never be used to submit information that someone knows to be false," the message said. "The District has zero tolerance for anyone who knowingly misuses the platform or participates in making a false threat. Any individual found responsible will face severe school disciplinary consequences and potential criminal charges." The principal concluded: "We appreciate your partnership in reinforcing that false threats are neither harmless nor funny. They place an unacceptable burden on students, employees, families, law enforcement and the broader community—and they must stop.Thank you for your immediate attention to this serious matter and for partnering with us to maintain a safe, orderly learning environment for every student and staff member at Martin County High School. Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Martin County Commission approved a zoning compromise for land in Hobe Sound, but the 3-2 vote has left some residents and at least one commissioner with lingering concerns about what could be built there.Commissioners voted to rezone a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said.Other residents echoed concerns about the scope of the original rezoning proposal."I understand that Martin County has to plan for the future but I also believe that growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists," Kim Call, a resident, said."We're concerned about the permanence of a GI classification which we believe is too broad and too open-ended," Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said.After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification."To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said.Despite the compromise, Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site."Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. A more unsettled weather pattern is setting up across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches for the middle and latter part of the week, bringing elevated chances for showers and thunderstorms, breezy northeast winds and a growing risk of rougher conditions at the beaches. An upper-level low approaching Florida from the western Atlantic is the feature behind the change. In simple terms, it will add energy higher in the atmosphere while pulling in deep tropical moisture at lower levels. That combination should make it easier for showers and storms to develop not just during the typical afternoon window, but at times earlier or later in the day as well. Wednesday will feature a mix of sun and clouds, with scattered showers and thunderstorms becoming more likely through the afternoon and evening. High temperatures will still reach the upper 80s to around 90 degrees, so it will remain warm and humid despite the increase in clouds and rain chances. Heat indices look to be a few degrees below the triple digits to near 100 degrees, a few degrees cooler than recently. A few storms could produce frequent lightning, brief heavy downpours and gusty winds. The storm coverage is expected to increase further Thursday and Friday as the upper-level low moves closer to the peninsula. Rain chances are elevated across both the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with numerous showers and thunderstorms possible at times. This does not mean the entire area will see nonstop rain or a complete washout, but outdoor plans could face interruptions, especially during the afternoon and evening. The main concern will be pockets of heavy rain. Storms may move slowly at times or repeatedly affect the same locations, raising the risk for localized street flooding and ponding water in poor-drainage areas. The severe-weather threat appears low overall, but isolated stronger storms could still bring gusty winds and plenty of cloud-to-ground lightning. Breezy easterly to northeasterly winds will also become more noticeable, particularly near the coast. Those winds may offer only limited relief from the humidity while creating choppier conditions along the Atlantic waters. For boaters, a Small Craft Advisory is in effect from this afternoon through late tonight for the entire Treasure Coast and Palm Beach coastal waters. Northeast to east winds are expected to increase to 15 to 20 knots, while seas build to 4 to 6 feet, occasionally reaching 8 feet offshore. Conditions in the Intracoastal Waterway will also become choppy in exposed areas. Beachgoers should use extra caution as the onshore flow increases. The National Weather Service has posted a Rip Current Statement for Atlantic beaches. Increasing onshore wind and building surf can create dangerous currents that pull swimmers away from shore, even when the weather appears calm between showers. By the weekend, the upper-level low should begin shifting west, allowing the weather pattern to gradually return toward more typical scattered afternoon storms.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police chief explains why both drivers face charges in road rage shooting on SW Brevity Terrace
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk released new details Monday about the road rage shooting Thursday evening near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace, clarifying why both drivers face felony charges despite one man being shot. The chief said the incident began as a misunderstanding during a lane change and escalated into violence that left one man injured and both arrested.

Police received a 911 call around 6:30 p.m. reporting gunshots in the residential neighborhood. Dean Plotts, 41, exited his vehicle and approached Tylon Kukielka, 57, who was seated in his car, and punched him through the window. Niemczyk said Plotts broke the plane of the window by entering the vehicle, which constitutes burglary of a conveyance with the intention of committing battery.

Plotts then returned to his vehicle, and Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. When asked if Kukielka's actions could be considered self-defense, Niemczyk said no. "It's not self-defense at that point. If Plotts had been coming at him at that point, the shooting may well have been justified, but it was actually just the reverse. He was fleeing from him," the chief said.

Both men now face felony charges stemming from the confrontation that began as a dispute over a lane merge near Southwest Crosstown Parkway. "Because one thought the other one may have cut the other one off when they were both turning into the same roadway. Again, no reason to be facing felony charges; let it go, let it go," Niemczyk said. A 911 caller described hearing the gunshots and seeing a man with blood on his hands immediately after the shooting.

cards.headline: Palm City man charged after SWAT standoff at Bessey Creek Trail home
cards.teaser: Devin Abbey, 38, faces three charges including a felony after a Saturday armed barricade incident on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail prompted a SWAT response. The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not publicly explained how the standoff was resolved.
cards.body:
A Palm City man is facing three charges, including a felony, after the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team resolved an armed barricade standoff Saturday at a home on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail.

Devin Abbey, 38, was booked at the Martin County Jail with his total bond set at $12,500. The sheriff's office has not released details of the specific charges he faces.

Deputies were called to a residence on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road Saturday following reports of shots fired outside the home, according to the sheriff's office. Additional calls indicated the incident was domestic-related and involved an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, authorities said.

The sheriff's office described Abbey as armed and dangerous Saturday and said he was contained inside the residence. Road patrol deputies, detectives, SWAT and the Hostage Negotiation Team responded to the scene. The sheriff's office asked people to avoid the area until further notice. The sheriff's office has not provided a public update on how the situation was resolved or whether anyone was taken into custody.

Officers located multiple bullet impacts on the exterior of the home. No injuries were reported.

hero.headline: Sheriff confirms former Fox News producer Jennifer Eckhart died by suicide in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Former Fox News producer Jennifer Eckhart was found dead in her Hobe Sound home Saturday morning in what authorities have confirmed was a suicide, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said during a news conference. A relative discovered Eckhart's body at her residence and contacted the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Budensiek described the scene as gruesome and horrific.

The sheriff said he typically does not comment on suicides but addressed rumors circulating about Eckhart's death, including speculation that she may have been murdered. Budensiek directly rebutted that speculation, explaining that the physical evidence made such theories impossible. He stated that based on the physical evidence in the house, it would be impossible for another human being to be in that space without leaving some type of fingerprint, shoeprint or some indication that another human was present.

Eckhart was perhaps most well known for accusing a Fox News anchor of raping her in 2020. The case was settled in 2024 before it went to trial. The circumstances surrounding her professional career at Fox News had kept her in the public eye in recent years.

Those experiencing a mental health crisis or who know someone in need of help can contact the Suicide Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988, or by accessing their online chat service. The 211 Helpline of Palm Beach and Treasure Coast is also available by dialing 211, or by texting a ZIP code to 898211. Mental health professionals are available through these services to provide support and resources to individuals in crisis.

hero.headline: Jolly refuses to debate Donalds, setting up Florida's first debate-free governor's race in 50 years
hero.body:
Democrat David Jolly said Sunday he will not debate Republican Byron Donalds before the Nov. 3 election, a decision that means Florida will hold its first governor's race without a televised debate in more than 50 years. The announcement triggered a new clash between the two major-party nominees, who accuse each other of avoiding voters.

Jolly announced his decision on MS NOW, telling Rev. Al Sharpton that Donalds acts in bad faith and continues to peddle lies. Donalds responded by pointing to Jolly's earlier willingness to debate him. The campaigns had accepted different debate invitations but never agreed to the same events. Jolly accepted proposed forums with CBS Miami's Jim DeFede and the Tampa Tiger Bay Club. Donalds announced he had accepted three other events involving Spectrum News and Florida A&M University, News4Jax, and Telemundo and NBC 6. Donalds' campaign said its proposed debates would feature two podiums and no audience. Jolly's campaign said it learned of those arrangements through a news release. Jolly said in a statement that Donalds refused the invitations Jolly had accepted and instead set his own rules by press release.

Jolly said Donalds is avoiding scrutiny of his property insurance proposal and other policies. Jolly's statement also linked to fact-checks of Donalds' campaign attacks. PolitiFact rated false a claim that Jolly wants higher taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security. Jolly is now citing reasoning Donalds used during the Republican primary, when Donalds declined calls to debate his primary opponents. At a Florida Chamber event, Donalds compared the campaign to applying for a job. Jolly said it is not his job to give Donalds a platform. He said his campaign has held more than 300 town halls and community meetings and will continue meeting voters and conducting online outreach.

Political analyst Dr. Susan MacManus said debates offer candidates free exposure and give voters, including those still undecided, a chance to compare the contenders directly. MacManus said declining interest in politics and lengthy televised events can reduce debates' appeal. Candidates may see more value in knocking on doors, holding town halls or doing local interviews. Artificial intelligence and social media add another consideration, she said. Misleading posts and manipulated material can spread while a debate is underway, potentially shaping perceptions before the candidates leave the stage. But refusing to participate can also alienate voters, MacManus said.

hero.headline: Indian River County's Operation Late Checkout nets over 50 arrests in human trafficking sting
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers.

Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office.

During the operation, several victims were identified, and ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. The arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online.

Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie advances $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B funding gap, phased fee hikes
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading Monday, advancing the city's 2050 Mobility Plan and an updated mobility-fee schedule that will increase development charges in phases between 2027 and 2030. The 25-year plan carries an estimated cost of approximately $2.2 billion, though approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded.

The updated fee schedule would increase charges paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders on new construction and certain property changes. The difference between current fees and newly calculated rates would be imposed in four steps: 25% of the increase in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full rate in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot single-family home east of Interstate 95, the mobility fee would increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. Developers could factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing infrastructure needs with the potential effect on housing affordability.

The short-term plan through 2030 carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million and includes widening St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard, widening Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard, and widening California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Other proposed short-term projects include widening St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line, continuing improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway, and widening Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. The plan also calls for building or extending several roads to improve connections through growing areas of the city.

Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. The program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3. The ordinance must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect in December.

cards.headline: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police charged a 37-year-old man with attempted aggravated battery and felony battery after he confronted another man with two knives in a restaurant parking lot and was shot Saturday afternoon.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police charged a 37-year-old man with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery after he confronted another man with two knives in a restaurant parking lot and was shot Saturday afternoon.

Christopher Harris faces the charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. Saturday.

A 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting.

The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm.

Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

hero.headline: Christopher Harris charged as primary aggressor after shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical
hero.body:
Police determined Christopher Harris was the primary aggressor in a Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical parking lot confrontation that ended with Harris shot in the upper torso and charged with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction.

Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department responded to the Pollo Tropical at 1635 NW St. Lucie West Blvd. on September 19 and found Harris suffering from gunshot wounds to his upper torso. The other person involved, identified as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while officers investigated. Police also recovered and secured a firearm.

Interviews and surveillance video from the restaurant showed the confrontation between Harris and Davis began after the two men had an interaction in the parking lot. Davis entered the restaurant to pick up a delivery order, and Harris followed him inside despite not appearing to place or pick up an order. When Davis left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Surveillance video showed Harris, who was armed with a knife, push Davis and then advance toward him as Davis backed away. Davis then pulled out a gun and fired one round, striking Harris in the upper torso.

Harris returned to the restaurant, where people began rendering aid and called 911. During the investigation, officers recovered one knife from Harris' waistband while aid was being provided and another from his front pocket. Harris was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Based on surveillance video, witness statements and other evidence, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor. Police said Harris will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail once he is medically released from the hospital.

hero.headline: Palm City SWAT standoff followed threats, gunfire and attempts to destroy evidence
hero.body:
A new arrest report reveals that Darrel Abbey threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend, fired shots outside his Palm City home, and attempted to wipe away evidence before an hours-long SWAT standoff with the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

According to the arrest report, Abbey's ex-girlfriend arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts and appeared to be extremely intoxicated.

The report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed. When Abbey picked up the gun again after the woman had taken it from him, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now," according to the report.

cards.headline: 11-year-old describes hearing gunshots as SWAT surrounded Palm City street during standoff
cards.teaser: An 11-year-old Palm City boy recounted hearing several gunshots from his neighbor's yard Saturday before deputies evacuated his family during an hours-long SWAT standoff.
cards.body:
An 11-year-old Palm City boy recounted hearing several gunshots from his neighbor's yard Saturday before deputies evacuated his family during an hours-long SWAT standoff on SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road. Gavin Ryan, who lives next door to where the standoff occurred, said the incident frightened him because such events do not typically happen in his neighborhood. His mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard, and SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded.

Martin County deputies responded to a domestic-related incident at the property Saturday and 38-year-old Darrel Abbey barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property. Deputies said Abbey was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol. SWAT officers and hostage negotiators spent hours trying to convince him to surrender.

Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. Tracy said he had never heard about a shooting in someone's neighborhood before a neighbor told him about the incident.

Hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and faces three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

cards.teaser: A charter bus caught fire Monday morning on I-95 in Martin County, closing all southbound lanes and snarling traffic. The driver, who was alone on the bus, escaped without injury.
cards.body:
A charter bus caught fire Monday morning on Interstate 95 in Martin County, prompting authorities to close all southbound lanes and launch an investigation into the cause.

The fire occurred around 11:20 a.m. on the southbound side of the interstate. Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene to extinguish the blaze.

The driver was the only person on the bus at the time of the fire and was able to escape the vehicle. No injuries were reported in the incident.

One southbound lane of I-95 has since reopened to traffic. Authorities continue to investigate what caused the charter bus to catch fire.

cards.headline: Molly's House in Stuart marks 30 years of housing families during medical treatment
cards.teaser: The nonprofit organization in Stuart's medical district has provided affordable lodging and support services to patients and families receiving treatment on the Treasure Coast for three decades.
cards.body:
Molly's House in Stuart is celebrating 30 years of providing affordable lodging and support services for patients and families receiving medical treatment on the Treasure Coast. The nonprofit organization in Stuart's medical district was founded to help families stay close to doctors, hospitals and treatment providers during difficult medical situations.

Leaders with Molly's House said the mission continues to focus on reducing stress for families facing long-term care and recovery. The organization provides affordable lodging for guests traveling for treatment and also offers a free cancer support program for residents. Demand for support services remains strong as more families seek affordable options near treatment centers across South Florida and the Treasure Coast.

Kate Wiegerink, a member of the Molly's House board of directors and Molly Sharkey's sister, said the organization also works to educate new doctors, nurses and community members about the services available to patients and families. The nonprofit is celebrating the milestone with an open house Monday at its facility on Osceola Street in Stuart. Community members are invited to tour the house and healing garden while learning more about the organization's history and programs.

In addition to housing support, Molly's House provides weekly free meals to residents to help ease food expenses and preparation during stressful medical situations. Businesses and individuals can become a "Chef for a Day" and provide an average of 28 meals. Brandi Patricio, whose son TJ received treatment, shared how the nonprofit has helped her family manage the financial and emotional challenges tied to ongoing medical care. Patricio said having access to affordable lodging reduces anxiety about housing costs during treatment and allows families to focus on recovery and care.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man charged after knife confrontation at Pollo Tropical ends with him being shot
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police have charged a 37-year-old man after surveillance footage and witness statements showed he was the aggressor in a knife confrontation that ended with him being shot outside a restaurant Saturday afternoon. No charges are pending against the 25-year-old shooter.

Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following the incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. Saturday.

Police said Harris followed the 25-year-old man into the restaurant despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself while the victim was picking up a food delivery order. When the victim left, Harris followed him outside. Surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting.

The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders provided aid and called 911. Officers found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso and he was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm.

Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman launches Chris's Place, free grief support community
cards.teaser: A Port St. Lucie woman who lost her husband in 2018 is building a new in-person grief support community on the Treasure Coast to fill what she saw as a gap in local resources.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie woman is launching Chris's Place, a free in-person grief support community on the Treasure Coast designed to help people navigating loss.

Stacey Comer created the community after her husband Chris died in 2018 following complications from a kidney transplant. As she learned to navigate life without him, Comer began to notice there wasn't one central place on the Treasure Coast where people experiencing grief could go to find support, resources and connection. She started asking herself a simple question: "Why isn't there an entity where all of this lives under?" That question became the foundation for Chris's Place.

Comer said grief can be difficult to understand until you experience it yourself. While friends and family often want to help, people who are grieving can still feel isolated. "You only sort of know it if you're in the club, and when you're in the club everyone wants to be so supportive and helpful," Comer said. Chris's Place is intended to give people a place to connect with others who understand what they're going through.

The community is not limited to people who have lost a spouse or immediate family member. Comer wants it to be available to anyone who has experienced a loss and needs support navigating what comes next. Right now, Comer is creating Chris's Place from the ground up. Her long-term vision is to create a physical space on the Treasure Coast where people can gather, find resources and connect with others who understand grief. "You are not alone. You feel alone because you think you're the only one feeling it, but you're not," Comer said. She wants other people on the Treasure Coast to have the kind of support she realized was missing during her own journey through grief.

hero.headline: Palm City man charged with felony domestic assault after SWAT standoff
hero.body:
A Palm City man is facing three charges, including a felony, after the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team resolved an armed barricade standoff at a home on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail. Devin Abbey, 38, was booked at the Martin County Jail with total bond set at $12,500.

Abbey faces aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill (domestic), a third-degree felony; battery, touch or strike (domestic), a first-degree misdemeanor; and use of a firearm under the influence of alcohol, a second-degree misdemeanor.

Deputies were called to a residence on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road Saturday following reports of shots fired outside the home, according to the sheriff's office. Additional calls indicated the incident was domestic-related and involved an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, authorities said.

hero.headline: Air Force confirms missing Eglin AFB attack drone recovered by Pensacola fishing charter
hero.body:
The Air Force confirmed that a drone went missing from testing at Eglin Air Force Base and was recovered by a fishing charter off the Florida Panhandle on Saturday. The drone appeared to be an FLM 136, a clone of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 attack drone that has played a key role in current combat operations.

Hot Spots Charters, a fishing charter company out of Pensacola, discovered the drone floating offshore near Eglin Air Force Base, home of the Air Force's 96th Test Wing. Charter captain Daniel Arsenault wrote on Facebook that the crew made the surprising catch during a six-hour trip Saturday.

An Eglin Air Force Base spokesperson told defense news site The War Zone that the base was conducting a test when the test article went down. The spokesperson would not specify the type of drone. Photos shared by Hot Spots Charters showed the drone missing its nose section and rear propeller, taking up the entire bow section of the fishing boat.

The drone appeared to be part of the Air Force's Low-cost Unmanned Combat Attack System, or LUCAS, program announced late last year. The LUCAS drones are clones of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 model. Manufactured by Arizona-based Spektreworks, the drones are 9.8 feet long, have a wingspan of 8.2 feet, and weigh 70 pounds. US Central Command announced in early March that LUCAS drones were being used in the war with Iran. Arsenault told CNN he came across the drone by chance while riding along offshore and saw it floating. The charter company later posted on Facebook that the drone had been retrieved, writing that black SUVs came and got their drone.
